newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Industry Council to try to cut merger thresholds.
newsitem.headline: Industry Council to try to cut merger thresholds.

text.p: European Union industry ministers will try on Thursday to agree on a proposal that would allow the EU's competition watchdog to catch more mergers and takeovers in its net, but Britain threatens to spoil the feast.
"If Britain makes concessions, France and Germany will also drop their reservations," a diplomat said.
The diplomat said it was unclear whether the British resistance was real or dictated by the upcoming general elections in which European issues have played a key role.

The Commission's proposal under discussion aims at gaining power over cross-border transactions currently under the turnover thresholds set in the merger regulation but which require regulatory approval in more than three EU states.

The Commission proposed last year that such transactions should fall under its power on the conditions that the combined worldwide turnover of the companies involved be between 2.0 billion and 5.0 billion European currency units and the Union turnover of at least two of the companies be between 100 million and 250 million Ecus each.
The higher thresholds currently determine whether a merger or acquisition falls under EU jurisdiction.

The 'multiple filings' proposal, as it is known, is seen as "the second-best solution" to a straightforward reduction of the turnover thresholds for all mergers and acquisitions which has failed to get the support of a sufficient number of countries.

Diplomats and Commission officials said Britain was proposing to reduce the worldwide turnover to 3.0 billion Ecus and that at least two of the companies involved should have a turnover of 30 million Ecus each in each of three countries.
The Netherlands, which currently holds the EU presidency, proposed a compromise which consists in lowering the British proposal to 2.5 billion Ecus and 25 million Ecus respectively.

It is unclear how many more deals would qualify for the fast-track, one-stop shop clearance under the EU's merger rules. But one source estimated that it was likely that only six more transactions would be caught with the British proposal, a figure which he said did not justify amending the existing rules.
Threshholds aside, the evil was also in the conditions that some countries, including Britain, wanted to attach to the new rules.
London particularly defended that the EU's merger rules should not apply to agreements between EU airlines and non-EU carriers, something which was opposed by all other governments, the sources said.

The move is a clear reference to the legal battle opposing the Commission and Britain over the power to vet the alliance between British Airways and AMR's American Airlines although any outcome would come to late to have any bearing on the case at stake.

Germany, also proposed that the Commission reserved the right to withdraw clearance or impose conditions on transactions currently reviewed under article 85 of the treaty of Rome if found to restrict fair competition at a later stage. The Commission has proposed to extend the merger regulation to so-called cooperative joint ventures -- now notified under article 85 -- something widely applauded by business circles.
Germany has indicated it would drop its proposal if a global compromise was within reach.
The proposal requires unanimous approval to become law.
